sections.title: From the Best of the Produce
sections.html:
It is a mitzva to separate terumot and ma'asrot from the best part of the produce, as it is stated (Bamidbar 18:32): "when you set apart its best (ḥelbo) from it" – "ḥelbo" is its best part. And if there is no kohen or Levi there, and there is a concern that by the time he brings the good, ripe produce to the kohen and the Levi it will spoil, it is preferable that he separate from produce that will keep for a long time, even though it is not the very best. If he transgressed and separated the inferior produce, what he did is done and his produce is permitted to be eaten (Mishna Terumot 2:4-6; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 5:1).

Today, when we are all considered impure and the kohanim cannot eat the terumot, all produce is considered entirely inferior with regard to terumot, and therefore it is permitted le-khatḥila (from the outset) to separate terumot from the inferior produce. But ma'aser rishon for the Levi and ma'aser ani must be separated from the good produce (SA YD 331:52; Bi'ur Ha-Gra 95; and see below in halakhot 10-11).1

The mitzva is to separate terumot and ma'asrot from produce of the same species, and if one separated terumah from produce of one species on behalf of another species, his terumah is void, and he must separate terumah again from produce of the same species. This is the rule: whatever are kilayim (forbidden mixtures) with one another – such that if they are vegetables, it is forbidden to sow them intermingled, and if they are trees, it is forbidden to graft them onto one another – they are two species, and one does not separate terumah from one on behalf of the other, even from the superior species on behalf of the less superior one. But if there is no prohibition of kilayim between them, it is permitted to separate terumah from one variety on behalf of another variety of the same species. For example, all kinds of grapes in their various colors, and all kinds of cabbage in their various colors – they are one species. Likewise, peach and nectarine – one species. But oranges and grapefruits – two species (Mishna Terumot 2:6; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 5:2-3; Mishpat Kohen 25; above 3, note 4).

sections.title: From Obligated Produce on Behalf of Exempt Produce, and Different Levels of Obligation
sections.html:
One does not separate from produce that is exempt from terumot and ma'asrot, such as produce from outside the Land and produce from which terumot and ma'asrot have already been separated, on behalf of produce that is obligated in terumot and ma'asrot. And likewise the reverse: one does not separate from obligated produce on behalf of exempt produce. And if one separated – he has done nothing, and he must separate terumot and ma'asrot again from the obligated produce (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 5:12).

Produce from two different places, regarding both of which there is a doubt whether they have been tithed – one should not separate from one on behalf of the other, lest he separate from tithed produce on behalf of untithed produce or the reverse.

One should not separate from produce that is obligated in terumot and ma'asrot by rabbinic law on behalf of produce that is obligated by Torah law. And likewise the reverse: one should not separate from produce obligated by Torah law on behalf of produce obligated by rabbinic law.

Produce obligated by Torah law is produce that the owner of the field grew for the needs of his household, or produce that a person bought from the owner of the field before its processing was complete, and completed its processing himself for the needs of his household. Produce obligated by rabbinic law is produce that the owner of the field grew in order to sell it, as well as produce that grew in an unperforated pot. (In the note the law of one who erred and separated from one on behalf of the other will be explained.)2

One does not separate from produce whose obligation depends on one rabbinic enactment on behalf of produce whose obligation depends on two rabbinic enactments, and likewise the reverse. That is, even though today the entire obligation of terumot and ma'asrot is rabbinic (below 12:11), one should not separate from grapes that a person harvested for eating at home on behalf of grapes that a person harvested for sale. After the fact, if one separated from one on behalf of the other – he has fulfilled his obligation.3

sections.title: Mukaf
sections.html:
It is a mitzva to separate terumah gedola from the mukaf (adjacent produce), that is, from produce that is near and adjacent to each other, such that it can be encompassed together. After the fact, one who separates terumah gedola not from the mukaf has fulfilled his mitzva (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 3:17, 20). Since terumat ma'aser is also called terumah, the Sages were accustomed to separate terumat ma'aser from the mukaf as well.4

If the produce is lying in an open field, one should bring it close together (SA YD 325:2). Produce lying within one room, even when part of it is on one side and part on the other side, the walls of the room make it mukaf. And even if it is lying in open vessels, the room combines it (SA 331:26).

When one is about to pack the produce in boxes, bottles or closed sacks, le-khatḥila one should separate terumot and ma'asrot from it beforehand, since some hold that fixed packaging separates between the foods and they are not considered mukaf together. When necessary, one may bring them close to each other and separate terumah also on behalf of the produce inside the packaging. However, barrels or bottles of wine, in which the wine continues to age and improve – since people are careful that they remain closed so as not to damage the wine, what is inside each barrel or bottle is separate unto itself and is not considered mukaf with its fellow, and therefore one must separate terumah on behalf of the wine before sealing it in barrels or bottles. Or else they should separate terumah from each and every barrel and each and every bottle after they are opened (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 3:18; SA 331:26).

For the sake of a mitzva, it is permitted to separate not from the mukaf. For example, one who knows that tevel produce is going to be brought to him on Shabbat or Yom Tov may, while it is still day, separate terumot and ma'asrot from produce in his possession on behalf of the produce that is going to be brought to him (Yevamot 93a). Likewise, one who mistakenly gave his fellow tevel produce, and is unable to notify him to tithe it, should tithe it from produce in his own possession, in order to save his fellow from eating tevel (Eruvin 32a).5

sections.title: How One Measures, and the Law of One Who Errs
sections.html:
In separating ma'asrot and terumat ma'aser, one should try to be precise, so as not to separate more than a tenth and not to separate less than a tenth. To this end one must measure produce whose volume is usually measured, and count produce that is usually counted, and best of all is to calculate by weight, which is the most precise (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 3:11; Hilkhot Ma'aser 1:14). After the fact, when it is not possible to weigh, measure or count the produce, he should separate the ma'asrot by estimate. And even if he errs greatly, as long as he intended to separate the proper measure and erred in the way people sometimes err – he has fulfilled his mitzva. But le-khatḥila the Sages instructed (Avot 1:16): "Do not tithe excessively by estimate."6

The accepted practice today (as will be explained further on) is that one does not actually separate produce for the ma'asrot, but only determines that a tenth of the produce lying on the south or north side shall be ma'aser. In this way the quantity of produce designated for ma'aser is precise. Afterward one gives their value to the Levi and to the poor person, and the produce of the ma'aser sheni one redeems on a peruta. However, the terumot, which are sacred, must actually be separated, and afterward one wraps them in order to place them respectfully in the garbage bin. For the terumot one must separate more than one-hundredth of the produce – one-hundredth for "terumat ma'aser," and the part beyond the hundredth for "terumah gedola." If one separated for the terumot exactly one-hundredth or less, it turns out that he did not separate "terumah gedola," since the terumah gedola is the part "beyond one-hundredth." And since it never occurred to him not to separate "terumah gedola" first, everything he did is void, and he must separate terumot and ma'asrot again in order (see Mirkevet Ha-mishneh and Yeshu'ot Malko on Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 13:19; Ma'adanei Eretz, Terumot 3:23:8).

The separation of terumot and ma'asrot has the same law as other vows and consecrations: if one regretted them, he may ask a Sage, together with two other people, to annul the separation for him according to the rules of annulling vows, and thereby the produce returns to its state of tevel (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 4:17. The same law applies to ḥalla, below 10:13 [?]).7

sections.title: The Law of Terumot in Our Times
sections.html:
Today, the kohanim may not eat pure terumah, since everyone is considered impure with the impurity of the dead, and we have no possibility of becoming purified from this impurity without the sprinkling of the water of the ashes of the red heifer. When the terumah is pure, it is forbidden to burn it or destroy it; rather, one must leave it until it decomposes on its own, or store it away by burial. When the terumah is impure, it is a mitzva to burn it so that people will not come to eat from it. However, it is difficult to burn it, and sometimes it is pure and it is forbidden to burn it, and a person does not always know whether it is pure. Therefore, the custom is to wrap the terumah and place it in the garbage bin, whether it is impure or pure, for in this way there is no concern that people will come to eat from it, and also one does not treat it with disrespect, since one places it wrapped.

When large quantities of terumah are involved, as long as it has not become impure, since it is forbidden to destroy it, one must leave it at the edges of the field until it decomposes on its own. And when there is a concern that people will come to eat it, it is proper to bury it or cover it a little with earth. And if it has become impure, it is a mitzva to burn it, and one may also bury it or compress it in a manner that it will be destroyed and people will not come to eat it.8

Terumah produce that became mixed with ḥullin produce of the same species is nullified in a hundred. And if they became mixed, one species with a different species, and he cannot separate the terumah from the mixture, for example because everything was mashed, the terumah is nullified in sixty. And if there was not the proportion necessary for the terumah to be nullified, one must treat the entire mixture as terumah (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 13:1-2). When necessary, just as vows are annulled, so too one may ask a Sage regarding the separation of the terumot and ma'asrot and annul it (as explained in the previous halakha).

sections.title: Using Terumot in Our Times
sections.html:
As we have learned (7:7), even though it is forbidden for a kohen to eat impure terumah, it is desirable that he benefit from it by way of burning. If the terumah is produce – he should fire the oven with it, and if it is oil – he should light the lamp with it. When the kohen lights for himself an oven for heating with impure terumah produce, or a lamp with impure terumah oil, it is also permitted for a Yisrael to benefit from it, for "a lamp for one is a lamp for a hundred." And even if the kohen afterward went on his way, the Yisrael may continue to benefit from the lamp or the oven that the kohen lit (Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 11:18). Just as it is forbidden to burn on Yom Tov the meat of sacrifices that became impure, so it is forbidden to burn impure terumah on Yom Tov; therefore, it is forbidden to light a lamp on Yom Tov with oil of impure terumah (Shabbat 24b).9

At the time when the kohanim could become pure and would eat terumah, the kohen was permitted to feed his animal only produce that was not fit for human consumption. And today, when it is forbidden for kohanim to eat terumah, a kohen is permitted to feed his livestock or his animals with terumah produce, whether the terumah is pure or impure. So that the terumah should not go to waste for nothing, some have the custom of transferring ownership of their livestock to a kohen who is a Torah scholar, and thus they can feed them the terumah that they separate for him. Afterward they settle accounts with the kohen and pay him what they saved in buying food for the animals.10

sections.title: A Kohen and a Levi Who Have Produce
sections.html:
Kohanim and Levites who have produce must separate terumot and ma'asrot from it like all Jews. But the kohen keeps the terumot in his possession and treats them with sanctity as required, and he also keeps the "ma'aser rishon" in his possession, for since he too is from the tribe of Levi, he has no obligation to bring it to a Levi. And a Levi who has produce separates terumot and ma'asrot from it as required, and keeps the "ma'aser rishon" for himself, and the terumot he gives to a kohen (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 1:3-4).

A kohen and a Levi who bought produce from a Yisrael after the work of its gathering was completed – the Sages penalized them, so that they do not separate terumot and ma'aser rishon for themselves but rather give them to other kohanim and Levites, so that they will not come to buy tevel produce from Yisraelim and deprive their brethren by taking the terumot and ma'aser rishon for themselves. However, if they bought the produce before its processing was complete, the terumot and ma'aser rishon are not taken from them (Yerushalmi Pe'ah 1:5; Rambam there 6:15).

Generally, the Levites would separate "terumat ma'aser" from the ma'aser they received, and they would also choose to which kohen to give it. But if the Yisrael wishes, he may separate "terumat ma'aser" from the ma'aser rishon that he separated for the Levi, and give it to a kohen together with the "terumah gedola," even though he thereby takes away from the Levi the right to choose to which kohen to give the "terumat ma'aser" from his ma'aser (Gittin 31a; Rambam, Hilkhot Terumot 3:12). Today, in order to prevent mishaps and forgetfulness, it is preferable that the Yisrael who separates the ma'aser immediately separate the "terumat ma'aser" as well, and place the terumot in the garbage bin, respectfully wrapped.

sections.title: Ma'aser Rishon in Our Times
sections.html:
As we have learned (above 7:8), it is a mitzva to give "ma'aser rishon" to a Levi. And although many hold that following the penalty that Ezra imposed on the Levites, it is permitted to give it to a kohen as well (Tosafot and Tur), since some hold that after the destruction of the Temple the penalty lapsed and the mitzva reverted to giving it specifically to a Levi, it is proper to satisfy all the poskim and give it specifically to a Levi (Rambam; SA YD 331:19; Mishpat Kohen 56).

Some argue that today there is no mitzva to give the "ma'aser rishon" to a Levi. And although it is obligatory to separate it by fixing a place for it – that it be on the north side of the produce and the like – in practice one need not give it. This is because, according to their argument, as a result of the upheavals of the exiles, the presumption of lineage was lost, and no person can prove that he is a member of the tribe of Levi, and consequently there is no obligation to give him the ma'aser (cited in Maharit 1:85). And some argue that as long as the presumption of lineage is not examined in a beit din, one may not rely on a person's word with regard to receiving gifts, so that there not be a proliferation of swindlers who will claim that they are Levites in order to receive the ma'aser (cited in Ḥazon Ish, Shevi'it 5:12). And some have the custom to be lenient on the basis of these arguments.

However, according to the overwhelming majority of the poskim, one must give "ma'aser rishon" to a Levi, because we rely on the tradition. Just as we rely on the tradition regarding kohanim, and give them the money of pidyon ha-ben (redemption of firstborn sons), and they go up to the platform to recite Birkat Kohanim, so too one should rely on the presumptive status of the Levites. And since in any case a person must separate ma'aser kesafim (a tithe of income), he should give the "ma'aser rishon" to a Levi who is a Torah scholar, and count it as part of "ma'aser kesafim" (as explained in the following halakhot).11

sections.title: Ma'aser Ani
sections.html:
In years 1, 2, 4 and 5 of the shemita cycle, one separates ma'aser sheni, and in years 3 and 6, ma'aser ani. Since the laws of ma'aser rishon and ma'aser ani are the same – they are ḥullin and are given in our times as in the past – we will deal first with the laws of ma'aser ani, and then complete the halakhot pertaining to both of these tithes.

A poor person too must separate "ma'aser ani" from his produce, and unlike a kohen and a Levi, who separate terumot and ma'aser rishon and keep them for themselves, the poor person must give the "ma'aser ani" to another poor person (Ḥullin 131b). Also a poor person who bought tevel produce must give the "ma'aser ani" to another poor person (Pe'at Ha-shulḥan 5, se'if katan 25). If his brother or his son was poor, as long as he is not separating in the field, he may give him all of it (above 7:11). Since this is so, it is preferable that he give the "ma'aser ani" to his relatives, for in the mitzva of tzedaka a person must give precedence to his relatives.

A poor person who is entitled to receive "ma'aser ani" is one who cannot obtain his basic needs according to what is accepted in that time and place. It seems that in a country that provides welfare budgets for the elderly and needy, the poor are those who are around the bottom tenth of the society in which they live, and in a country that does not provide welfare budgets, the percentage of the poor can reach a fifth of the entire public; but it is not plausible that more than a tenth or a fifth of the entire public would be considered poor, unless we are speaking of years of famine.

One may give "ma'aser ani" produce or its monetary value to a gabbai tzedaka (charity administrator) for the needs of the poor (Mishna Ma'aser Sheni 5:9). Likewise, one may give "ma'aser ani" to a yeshiva that supports young men and avreikhim (married yeshiva students) who live modestly and whose parents do not have money to support them. And even though young men and avreikhim who are helped by their parents and live comfortably also study there, they should direct that the "ma'aser ani" money be allocated to the support of the poor young men and avreikhim.

After the poor person has received the "ma'aser ani" produce, he may eat it or sell it and buy whatever he wishes with the proceeds. But it is forbidden to take it out of the Land, as it is stated (Devarim 26:12): "that they may eat within your gates and be satisfied" (Sifrei there; Arukh Ha-shulḥan, Zera'im 14:18). If he took it out, after the fact he may eat it outside the Land (see Pe'at Ha-shulḥan 12, se'if katan 27).

sections.title: The Manner of Giving the Ma'aser to the Levi and the Poor in Practice
sections.html:
The "ma'aser rishon" for the Levi, and the "ma'aser ani" that is separated in the third and sixth years – these are the tithes that are eaten by their recipients even today, because they are ḥullin and need not be eaten in purity. The measure of each of these tithes is about 9% of the produce. For we have learned that today one separates any amount whatsoever for "terumah gedola"; it turns out that even after its separation, the amount of produce remains as it was. Afterward one separates "ma'aser rishon" for the Levi, and from it one separates a tenth for the kohen, which is called "terumat ma'aser." It turns out that the part belonging to the Levi is about 9% of the produce. Afterward, in the third and sixth years, one separates "ma'aser ani" from the remaining produce, and its measure too is about 9% of all the produce, for after subtracting the "ma'aser rishon," 90% of the produce remains, and a tenth of that is 9%.

When the owner of the produce can bring the ma'aser produce to the Levi and the poor person – very good. However, today it is very difficult to distribute the ma'aser produce. For the mitzva is that when the owner of the produce finishes gathering his produce from the field, he separates terumot and ma'asrot, and the kohen, the Levi and the poor person come to him, and he gives each one his portion. And if they did not come, the Sages instituted that the owner of the field or his worker should bring it to their homes, and they pay him the customary wage for this (above 7:5). Today, most fruit growers are farmers who have large areas and whose yield is enormous, and if the farmer brings all his ma'aser produce to one Levi and one poor person, they will have no place to store it and will not know how to sell it. And if the farmers hire workers to distribute the ma'aser produce to Levites and poor people, in a quantity suited to the household consumption of each one, the payment they would pay for this distribution would be higher than the monetary value of the ma'aser produce they would receive. And then the Levites and the poor would prefer that the ma'aser produce, which entails a high payment for its transport, not be brought to them.

In order to fulfill the mitzva in a beneficial way, in accordance with its purpose, the owners of the produce should separate the ma'asrot for the Levi and the poor person, and afterward buy the produce from them with money, and give them the money. Le-khatḥila the owner of the produce must perform an act of acquisition (kinyan) so that the "ma'aser rishon" produce passes into the possession of a particular Levi, and the "ma'aser ani" produce into the possession of a particular poor person, and afterward buy the produce from them (as explained in the note). Or he can do this by means of a prior arrangement, by way of "makirei levi'ya" and "makirei ani" (acquaintances of a Levi or poor person) (as explained in the next halakha). After the fact, even when they did not perform an act of acquisition and did not arrange this in advance, the owner of the produce must convert the ma'aser produce into money, and afterward give this sum to the Levi and the poor person. And even though he did not receive permission from a particular Levi and a particular poor person to convert the produce into money, this falls under the category of returning a lost object, for by buying the ma'aser produce he saves it from destruction (Ḥullin 134b; Rambam, Hilkhot Bikkurim 9:16).12

sections.title: Giving the Ma'asrot in Practice to Acquaintances among Levites and the Poor
sections.html:
One of the good ways of fulfilling the mitzva of giving the ma'asrot in our day is that the owner of the produce arranges in advance with a Levi who is a Torah scholar that he will receive the "ma'aser rishon" from him, and gives the Levi a monetary loan against the ma'asrot that he will separate in the coming year. Through this, this Levi becomes his "makir levi'ya," that is, a Levi known as the one who receives his ma'asrot, and then, immediately after the separation of the ma'aser, the ma'aser produce passes into his possession without the need for an act of acquisition. And each time the owner of the produce separates ma'aser, he should calculate its value and deduct it from the loan that the Levi owes him, and thereby the ma'aser produce returns to his possession. When the price of the ma'aser produce reaches the value of the loan, the loan is erased, and the owner of the produce again gives an additional loan to the Levi, and again deducts the value of the ma'asrot from the sum of the loan. One can do the same with a poor person regarding "ma'aser ani" (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 7:5-6).

For repaying the loan, the price of the produce is calculated according to the cheap market rate of the produce, so that if at the beginning of the season its price is high and in the middle of the season it is low, the price of the produce should be calculated throughout the season according to its low rate. And there is no ribbit (prohibited interest) in this, since this is not an ordinary loan, but a loan that serves as an advance payment for the ma'aser produce, and its repayment depends on the value of the ma'aser produce, and if there is no ma'aser produce against it, the loan will be erased (Gittin 30a; Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser 7:7).13

sections.title: Ma'aser Sheni and Its Redemption
sections.html:
The mitzva of eating "ma'aser sheni" produce in purity within the walls of Jerusalem depends on the existence of the Temple (above 7:9); therefore today, when the Temple is destroyed, even if we could become purified from the impurity of the dead, we would have no possibility of eating the "ma'aser sheni" produce. Nevertheless, it is obligatory to separate terumot and ma'asrot, including "ma'aser sheni," because the mitzva of separation does not depend on the existence of the Temple (Rambam, Hilkhot Ma'aser Sheni 2:1). However, there is no need for the "ma'aser sheni" produce to go to waste, because the Torah established that the "ma'aser sheni" produce can be redeemed for money, and thereby the sanctity passes to the money and the produce is permitted to all. And although the Torah's commandment is to redeem it for its value plus a fifth, after the fact, if one redeemed it for a peruta, the produce is deconsecrated. And since today the redemption money goes to waste, le-khatḥila one may redeem it for one peruta, and this is indeed what it is worth, since it is impossible to benefit from it (Rambam 2:2; 4:18).

With less than the value of a peruta it is impossible to redeem the produce, because it has no significance, and therefore it is impossible to perform an acquisition or redemption with it. The value of a peruta is the value of 1/45 of a gram of silver. Since the price of silver is subject to fluctuations, the value of the peruta rises and falls (in recent years the value of the peruta has generally been about four to five agorot).

When necessary, one may redeem "ma'aser sheni" produce onto food worth a peruta, wrap it, and place it respectfully in the garbage bin, just as one places terumah. But le-khatḥila one should redeem "ma'aser sheni" produce onto money.

A person who wishes to redeem "ma'aser sheni" produce from time to time onto a peruta must designate a coin for this, and if the price of the peruta remains about five agorot, as it is today, he can redeem onto a five-shekel coin one hundred times, and onto a ten-shekel coin two hundred times. In order to remember that this is the coin designated for this, it is proper to mark it with a sticker.14

This is the order of the redemption: after finishing the separation, one recites the blessing: "Blessed are You, Lord our God, King of the universe, who has sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to redeem ma'aser sheni," and says: "This ma'aser sheni, it and its fifth, is deconsecrated onto one peruta of the coin that I have designated for the redemption of ma'aser sheni." And if he deconsecrates it onto food, he says: "This ma'aser sheni, it and its fifth, is deconsecrated onto this food," and places it wrapped in the garbage bin, so that it will not be treated with disrespect.

sections.title: Some Laws of Redemption
sections.html:
When one redeems "ma'aser sheni" onto money, one must redeem it onto a coin that is in circulation in that place, and not onto a coin that is not in circulation there, since it is not considered money there (Rambam 4:9-10).

A person may permit his family members and friends to redeem "ma'aser sheni" produce that they have onto the coin that he designated for this, provided that he estimates that they will not exceed the number of perutot that his coin is worth. And if he is in doubt, he can designate two coins for this, one of ten shekels and one of five shekels (and it is good to stick them together in order to mark them), and give everyone permission to deconsecrate onto a peruta of the large coin; and every so often, as needed, he deconsecrates all the perutot of the large coin onto one peruta of the small coin. He should do so until the time of "bi'ur ma'asrot" (removal of tithes) arrives, at which time he deconsecrates all the perutot of the large and small coins onto a piece of fruit, or wine or oil, worth a peruta. Afterward he can use these coins again for the coming years. If he redeemed the perutot onto a piece of fruit or food, he should place it wrapped respectfully in the garbage bin. And if he redeemed onto wine or oil, he should pour them into the sink, but not into the toilet.15

When a person redeems his "ma'aser sheni" produce onto his fellow's coin, he does not add a fifth, but says: "This ma'aser sheni shall be deconsecrated onto a peruta of the coin that so-and-so designated for the redemption of ma'aser sheni" (Rambam 5:1, 8).

When "ma'aser sheni" produce is worth less than four perutot, since the value of the fifth is less than the value of a peruta, one does not add a fifth, and he says: "This ma'aser sheni shall be deconsecrated onto a peruta of the coin that I have designated for the redemption of ma'aser sheni" (Rambam 5:4). If he erred and added a fifth in a case where he did not need to add it – he has fulfilled his obligation.16

sections.title: One Does Not Redeem When the Value Is Less Than a Peruta, Nor in Jerusalem
sections.html:
If the value of the "ma'aser sheni" is less than a peruta, it is impossible to redeem it (Bava Metzia 53b), because whatever is worth less than a peruta has no significance such that an act of acquisition or redemption can be performed with it. And since it is impossible to redeem it, and it is also forbidden to eat it, destroy it or treat it with disrespect, one must wrap it and place it in the garbage bin, as is done with terumot. And one who wishes to be lenient can decide in his mind that as far as he is concerned it is worth a peruta, and redeem it onto a peruta. But the idea of a "peruta ḥamura" (stringent peruta) is strained and of no benefit, and therefore one should not use it, as explained in the note.17

One does not redeem pure ma'aser sheni produce in Jerusalem, that is, within the ancient walls of sanctified Jerusalem, including the City of David and Mount Zion, which were within the walls.18 For the whole reason the Torah permitted redeeming produce for money is in order to bring it up to Jerusalem, as it is stated (Devarim 14:24-25): "And if the way be too long for you, so that you are not able to carry it … then you shall turn it into money, and bind up the money in your hand, and go to the place which the Lord your God shall choose"; from here [we learn] that if the produce is already in Jerusalem – it is forbidden to redeem it. And if he redeemed it – the redemption is void (Yerushalmi Ma'aser Sheni 1:3; Rambam 2:4; Yeshu'ot Malko). Rather, he should place the "ma'aser sheni" produce that he separated in Jerusalem in a hidden place until it rots, and if it is a small amount, he should wrap it and place it in the garbage bin, as is done with terumot.19
